//: Shared-hosting profile (myASP.NET and anything else that is ASP.NET Core on IIS). Values that are secret belong in the host's environment variables, not in this file — it is committed. An environment variable overrides the matching key here: ConnectionStrings__DefaultConnection beats ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection.

ConnectionStrings.//DefaultConnection: Set as an environment variable on the host, or paste the MSSQL connection string the control panel issues. It contains a password, so it does not live here. Encrypt=True unless the host says otherwise; TrustServerCertificate=True only if their certificate is not one you can validate.
ConnectionStrings.//DefaultConnection-scale: Past roughly a hundred concurrent tills, add 'Max Pool Size=400;Min Pool Size=10'. ADO.NET caps a pool at 100 connections by default and then queues, so the first symptom of outgrowing it is not an error but every till going slow at once. Raise SQL Server's own 'user connections' to match, and remember the ceiling is per instance: four API instances at 400 each is 1600 connections asking one database for room.
ConnectionStrings.//Redis: Only read when Cache:Provider is Redis, and ignored entirely under SqlServer. A shop moving to more than one API instance sets both this and Cache:Provider together — see Cache:Provider.

Cache.//Provider: Redis, SqlServer or InMemory — and the choice is really 'what does this host have, and how many instances'. InMemory is refused outright in Production, because two instances each holding their own carts and tag claims can tell two tills the same tagged item is theirs and let both sell it, with nothing on any screen to say so.
Cache.//Provider-SqlServer: For hosting that offers a database and nothing else — shared IIS, in particular. Cart state, tag claims, idempotency records and hub tickets go in the application's own database, and every guarantee the Redis version makes is kept: the tag claim is a primary key settled by a single MERGE under HOLDLOCK, and a hub ticket is redeemed by DELETE … OUTPUT, so neither can be won twice. It costs a database round trip on paths that used to hit memory, and it needs no second service to be up. One thing does not carry over: there is no SignalR backplane, so a hub message published by one instance does not reach a till connected to another. SqlServer means one instance.
Cache.//Provider-Redis: The answer wherever there is a Redis to point at, and the only answer past one instance — the backplane is what keeps a second cashier's screen in step.

Database.//AutoMigrate: False. Migrating from inside the web process means the first request after a deploy races the schema change, and on shared hosting several worker processes may start at once. Run `dotnet ef database update` against the host's database from a machine you control, then deploy.

Jobs.//RunServer: False on shared IIS. The Hangfire worker is a background loop, and the pool that hosts it is recycled on a schedule and unloaded when idle — so the nightly late-charge accrual would run only if somebody happened to be using the site at 2am. Storage stays registered either way, so the schedule and its history are still visible. Drive the job from something that is awake: the host's task scheduler, or an uptime pinger against the trigger endpoint.
Jobs.//RunServer-scale: Running several API instances: leave this true on exactly one of them. Hangfire's SQL storage takes a lock per job so duplicates are not the danger — wasted workers polling the same tables are, and one instance owning the schedule is easier to reason about when a nightly job did not run.

ServerReaders.//Enabled: Only where the server can route to the readers. Behind a load balancer, every instance would open its own connection to the same reader — and a UHF bridge accepts one client, so instances would fight over it. Either pin reader hosting to one instance, or run the terminal agent on each till and leave this off.

OpenIddict.//AllowInsecureHttp: Absent, which means HTTPS is required. An authorization code or a bearer token crossing the public internet in the clear is the whole attack.
OpenIddict.//SigningCertificatePath: Required. Outside Development the application refuses to start without both certificates rather than falling back to development keys — those live in the launching user's certificate store, which a shared IIS pool does not load, so they would be regenerated on every recycle and sign the whole shop out at intervals nobody could account for. Generate a pair, upload them, and point these at the .pfx files.
OpenIddict.//CertificatePassword: Set as an environment variable (OpenIddict__CertificatePassword) if the .pfx files are protected.

Auth.//WebOrigin: The public origin the front end is served from, exactly as the browser sees it — scheme, host, no trailing slash. It is the redirect target after sign-in and part of the content security policy, so a mismatch shows up as a login that appears to fail while succeeding.
Auth.//AdminPassword: Environment variable only (Auth__AdminPassword). A seeded credential written into a committed file is a published credential.

Serilog.//WriteTo: File paths must stay inside the application's own folder. A shared pool identity has no rights to ProgramData or a user profile, and a sink that cannot open its file takes the logging pipeline down with it.
